segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I was given a reed like a rod, and I was told,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Get up and measure the sanctuary of God and the altar and those who worship in it.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But leave out the court outside the sanctuary and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I will grant it to my two witnesses to prophesy for one thousand two hundred sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if anyone wants to harm them, fire comes out of their mouth and devours their enemies; if anyone should want to harm them, this is how that person must be killed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have the authority to shut the sky, so that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have authority over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war on them and conquer them and kill them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And their corpses will lie on the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And some from among the peoples and tribes and languages and nations look at their corpses for three and a half days, and they do not allow their corpses to be placed in a tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who live on the earth rejoice over them and celebrate, and they will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who live on the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who were watching them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come up here!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went up to heaven in the cloud, and their enemies watched them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell, and seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest became terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second woe has passed. Look, the third woe is coming soon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the twenty-four elders who sit before God on their thrones fell on their faces and worshiped God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The nations grew angry, and your anger has come, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for giving the reward to your slaves the prophets and to the holy ones and to those who fear your name, the small and the great, and for destroying those who destroy the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the sanctuary of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his sanctuary, and there came flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder and an earthquake and heavy hail.

notes.note: Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here, for the building where God dwells. Most English versions render both as “temple.” The distinction matters in this passage, because the outer court in verse 2 lies outside what is measured.

notes.traditional: and the angel stood, saying (KJV); and I was told (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek has only a participle, “saying,” with no stated speaker. The voice goes on to say “my two witnesses” in verse 3, which suggests God or Christ, or an angel speaking for them. Where the speech ends is also uncertain; it is closed here after verse 3, as in most versions, though some extend it further.

The same Greek word is translated “nations” in verses 9 and 18. It means peoples in general and, in the plural, often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. “Gentiles” is used here because the image is of the temple’s outer court and the holy city handed over to foreigners; “nations” is equally possible.

Forty-two months, the one thousand two hundred sixty days of verse 3, and three and a half years are the same span. It echoes the “time, times, and half a time” of Daniel (7:25; 12:7), a limited period in which God’s people are oppressed. The three and a half days of verses 9 and 11 mirror the figure on a small scale.

notes.phrase: the two olive trees and the two lampstands
notes.note: The image comes from Zechariah 4, where two olive trees stand beside a golden lampstand and are identified as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. In Zechariah’s setting these are usually understood as the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua.

The powers described recall Elijah, who announced a drought and called down fire (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 1), and Moses, who turned water into blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). Whether the two witnesses are meant as these figures returned, as other individuals, or as a symbol of the witnessing church is disputed.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a victory in battle or in a contest. “Overcome” in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty, and it hides the link with the promises to “the one who conquers” elsewhere in Revelation. The meaning is not disputed; several modern versions also use “conquer” here.

notes.traditional: spiritually (KJV); symbolically, figuratively or prophetically (modern versions)
notes.note: The adverb signals that the names Sodom and Egypt are not literal, but belong to the Spirit’s way of seeing the city; modern versions paraphrase as “symbolically” or “prophetically.” The reference to the crucifixion points to Jerusalem, yet “the great city” elsewhere in Revelation is Babylon. Many interpreters therefore take it as a composite image of the world city opposed to God.

The Greek shifts here from future verbs to the present tense (“look,” “do not allow,” “rejoice,” “celebrate”) and then back to the future (“will send”). Most versions smooth everything into the future. The shifts are kept here because they are in the Greek, where the vision slips between prediction and vivid description.

notes.traditional: the Spirit of life (KJV); a breath of life (ESV, NRSV)
notes.note: The Greek word means both “breath” and “spirit.” The wording echoes Ezekiel 37, where breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, so “breath” is used here. “A spirit of life from God” is also possible.

notes.traditional: which art, and wast, and art to come (KJV)
notes.note: Some later manuscripts add “and who is to come,” matching the fuller title in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, and the King James Version follows them. The earliest and best witnesses lack the phrase. Its absence fits the context: the hymn celebrates that God has now come to reign.

notes.phrase: The nations grew angry, and your anger has come
notes.traditional: The nations raged (or were angry), and your wrath has come
notes.note: The Greek uses a verb and a noun from the same root, setting the nations’ anger against God’s. Most versions use “wrath” for God’s anger and so lose the echo. The line recalls Psalm 2, where the nations rage against the Lord and his anointed, the same psalm that lies behind “our Lord and his Christ” in verse 15.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, and not for a hired servant. “Your servants the prophets” is a set Old Testament phrase and most versions keep “servants.” In that phrase the word is a title of honor for those wholly at God’s disposal, but a first-century reader still heard the word for a slave.

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many versions keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

candidates.reason: Translators split between “slave” and “servant” across the whole New Testament, and the Old Testament phrase “your servants the prophets” makes the choice especially visible.
“Wrath” is traditional and “anger” is the plain modern equivalent; here the cognate verb forces a choice, and the word recurs in Paul, John and Revelation.
Versions vary between “abyss,” “bottomless pit” and “the deep” across Luke 8:31, Romans 10:7 and Revelation, and readers should see it is one term.
“Testimony” and “witness” alternate in English for this noun and its cognates throughout John, the Johannine letters and Revelation, where the word group is thematic.
The word means a blow or wound and, in Revelation, a plague; a single decision is needed on when it is “plague,” “blow” or “wound” so the Exodus echoes stay visible.
